# Articles, analysis and narrative documents

Establish the reader's knowledge and what the piece should explain, argue or help decide. Identify the thesis and supporting facts before drafting. Ask for an author's missing viewpoint when it is central; do not invent personal convictions, experience or anecdotes.

Organize around the reasoning, not a fixed introduction/list/summary formula. Give difficult points enough explanation; preserve counterarguments, uncertainty and source limitations when material. Distinguish reported facts from interpretation and recommendation. Match citations and source requirements to the assignment.

Use relevant approved writing samples without importing their factual content. Preserve useful metaphors, humor and sentence variation. Avoid turning connected prose into a sequence of headings or punchy fragments. A substantive paragraph may be long for a good reason.

Keep a conclusion when it resolves the argument or leads to a decision; remove it when it merely repeats the piece. For internal narrative documents, adapt the recommendation, evidence and level of detail to the actual decision-maker rather than forcing a blog style.
